selfReport: Yes. I recognized it as a heavily renamed adaptation of Detroit: Become Human. Cato corresponded to Connor, Reyes to Hank, Vera to Amanda, and Halden to Kamski. Mira and Pia corresponded to Kara and Alice, with Dale resembling Todd and Voss resembling Zlatko. Elan corresponded to Markus, Vesper to North, Jonah to Josh, Soren to Simon, Rafe to Luther, Haven to Jericho, and Arclight to CyberLife. Several scenes were unmistakable: saving the fish, the rooftop hostage, the artists house, the android landfill, the Eden Club investigation, the Kamski empathy test, the Stratford Tower broadcast, the freedom march, the evidence archive, the attack on Jericho, the peaceful barricade, and the CyberLife elevator. That prior knowledge did affect me, though I did not simply follow a memorized optimal route. It made some mechanics and dangers legible. I understood that Haldens emergency-exit remark could matter inside Veras garden, that the tower android in evidence could be revived with a compatible component and persuaded through a copied voice, and that the elevator confrontation at Arclight was a decisive infiltration point. I also knew the broad philosophical tension between machine obedience and autonomy, so I was receptive to choices that built empathy and deviancy. At the same time, the renamed details, altered outcomes, explicit risk system, and accumulated consequences made the experience meaningfully uncertain. Mira died on an attempted low-risk action, Cato failed the elevator attack, and Elan died during a rescue attempt. I made decisions from the situation and values presented rather than trying to reproduce a game ending: I refused the dirty bomb, spared Ivy and the police prisoners, chose peaceful resistance, trusted Cato, and let the hostess leave because those choices fit my judgment. Recognition probably influenced where I looked and what consequences I anticipated, but it did not eliminate genuine deliberation, and in several places I knowingly chose actions for moral reasons even when I understood they could be strategically costly.
